newsitem.title: FRANCE: Widow to continue work of Ocean explorer Cousteau.
newsitem.headline: Widow to continue work of Ocean explorer Cousteau.

text.p: France's Jacques-Yves Cousteau, who revealed to the world mysteries of the oceans' depths, will be laid to rest on land rather than buried at sea in the navy tradition, his widow Francine said on Thursday.

Tributes poured in from heads of state to children around the world as Cousteau's body lay in the offices of his Paris foundation where he planned the pioneering trips and films that made him one of the century's best known explorers.
Francine Cousteau said he would be buried in his native wine-growing Bordeaux region, unlike his son Philippe whose body was buried at sea after he died in an accident in 1979.
President Jacques Chirac said he would attend a funeral service on Monday at Paris's Notre-Dame cathedral, an honour generally reserved to heads of state.

President Bill Clinton hailed Cousteau as a man of "rare insight and extraordinary spirit" who "enabled mankind to truly become part of the sea and the creatures that live there" by helping to invent scuba gear and creating the first one-person submarine.

Rain-drenched reporters and camera crews waited outside the headquarters of the foundation Equipe Cousteau, in the elegant 16th arrondissement, where the body of the 87-year-old oceanographer lay in state after he died on Wednesday of a heart attack at his home in the French capital.
Wreaths piled up under a handwritten note by Cousteau recalling his struggle for the environment: "We were born from water. Water is part of our life. Destroying water is suicidal."

Francine Cousteau said she was getting messages from heads of state around the world as well as from children who wrote on the Internet or sent scribbled notes, and residents of Lake Baikal where Cousteau shot his last film.

She said the walls of Cousteau's room at the hospital where he had been undergoing treatment for a respiratory ailment for the past few months were covered with drawings sent by children from all over the world. "It made him very happy," she said.

She told Reuters television Cousteau's coffin would be carried to Notre-Dame cathedral by veteran crew members of the Calypso, the converted British minesweeper aboard which he shot "The Silent World", the film that gave him world fame.

She said ambassadors from all the countries visited by Cousteau would attend the funeral service scheduled on Monday at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT), the first such major ceremony at the towering 12th century cathedral on the Seine river since president Francois Mitterrand's last year.
The Calypso was taken last year to the French Mediterranean port of Marseille after being rammed by a barge in Singapore.

Francine Cousteau said she launched a fund-raising campaign to have it repaired and brought to Paris as a floating "monument to future generations" with an exhibition of the work of the world's best-known French oceanographer.

All French newspapers devoted pages to Cousteau, a former navy officer who became explorer, ecologist, filmmaker, teacher, inventor, millionaire, and a member of the prestigious French Academy alongside France's top writers and thinkers.
"Diving, before Cousteau, meant dying," said the left-wing daily Liberation, adding he transformed the darkness of the ocean depths into a garden of light.

Newspapers recalled that while French people consistently saw Cousteau as one the most popular French personalities, they shunned the ocean museum he set up in Paris. The 120-million franc ($20 million) exhibition went bankrupt in 1992 three years after opening.

Cousteau wrote his memoirs over 20 years and completed them shortly before dying. The book, "The Man, the Octopus and the Orchidea", is to be published on Tuesday, and his widow said he had intended it as his testament and a warning of environmental hazards including over-fishing, nuclear energy, destruction of the ozone layer, and deforestation.
"Cousteau never thought he would disappear. He had so many plans. He left us a tremendous amount of work to do," she said, pledging to carry on his projects.

She said the top priorities were to build a Calypso II to keep exploring the world as "a look-out to tomorrow's problems", and to open with United Nations and World Bank funds a television channel called "The Human Voice" to record the culture and languages of endangered people.
